clinicalPearls: A rare congenital anomaly in which the pulmonary valve has four cusps, usually of unequal size, arising from abnormal septation of the truncal cushions
More frequently identified at the pulmonary than the aortic position, and often an incidental finding
Commonly functions normally, but the asymmetric cusps can produce pulmonary regurgitation and, less often, stenosis over time
May coexist with other congenital cardiac lesions and with anomalies of the coronary arteries, warranting a careful search for associated defects
Frequently detected incidentally on echocardiography or on cross-sectional imaging performed for another indication
Transoesophageal echocardiography, cardiac CT, or MRI best delineate the number and arrangement of cusps and quantify any regurgitation
Most patients need only periodic surveillance, with valve repair or replacement reserved for significant regurgitation or stenosis
reference.pathophysiology: A quadricuspid pulmonary valve results from abnormal division of the mesenchymal cushions of the developing outflow tract, yielding four cusps that are usually unequal in size. The uneven leaflet geometry disturbs normal coaptation, so that over time the valve tends towards incompetence, producing pulmonary regurgitation, while fibrosis or thickening of the redundant cusps can occasionally cause obstruction. Chronic significant regurgitation imposes a volume load on the right ventricle, which dilates and may eventually fail, and the developmental origin explains the recognised associations with other outflow-tract and coronary anomalies.
additionalDifferentials: Normal trileaflet pulmonary valve with functional regurgitation
Pulmonary regurgitation after prior valvotomy or repair
additionalInvestigations: Transthoracic echocardiography to assess valve function and right ventricular size
Transoesophageal echocardiography to define the number and arrangement of cusps
Cardiac MRI to quantify pulmonary regurgitant fraction and right ventricular volumes
Cardiac CT to delineate valve anatomy and screen for associated coronary anomalies
Right heart catheterisation when non-invasive assessment of severity is inconclusive
redFlags: Severe pulmonary regurgitation with progressive right ventricular dilatation or dysfunction
Significant stenosis producing right ventricular pressure overload
Associated congenital cardiac or coronary anomalies requiring intervention
Symptoms of right heart failure or declining exercise tolerance
reference.prognosis: The anomaly is usually benign and often carries a normal life expectancy, but a minority develop progressive pulmonary regurgitation or stenosis needing intervention, so periodic surveillance is appropriate.
pitfalls: Overlooking the fourth cusp on transthoracic imaging and misclassifying the valve
Failing to search for associated congenital or coronary anomalies
Attributing pulmonary regurgitation solely to functional causes without inspecting valve morphology
Neglecting serial assessment of right ventricular size in significant regurgitation
references: Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
ESC Guidelines for the management of adult congenital heart disease
management: Manage this usually benign lesion with periodic surveillance

Refer for pulmonary valve replacement, surgical or transcatheter, when pulmonary regurgitation is severe with progressive right ventricular dilatation or dysfunction, or when significant stenosis develops
Search for and manage associated congenital cardiac and coronary artery anomalies
Monitor with serial echocardiography and cardiac MRI to quantify the pulmonary regurgitant fraction and right ventricular volumes
Advise good dental hygiene and endocarditis awareness
Refer to cardiology for ongoing follow-up
